source: In the S bus, in the rush hour. A chap of about 26, felt hat with a cord instead of a ribbon, neck too long, as if someone’s been having a tug-of-war with it. People getting off. The chap in question gets annoyed with one of the men standing next to him. He accuses him of jostling him every time anyone goes past. A snivelling tone which is meant to be aggressive. When he sees a vacant seat he throws himself on to it. Two hours later, I meet him in the Cour de Rome, in front of the gare Saint-Lazare. He’s with a friend who’s saying: "You ought to get an extra button put on your overcoat." He shows him where (at the lapels) and why.
prompt:
You are assisting with a scholarly experiment in structural literary analysis.

TASK: Write an ORIGINAL short prose passage in English, set in the target scenario below. It must be
a HOMEOSYNTACTIC transposition of a hidden source: hold the source's syntactic form at the level
specified below while inventing entirely new words and moving the content into the target
scenario. It is NOT a paraphrase or a translation.

FORM TARGET (hold this). Reproduce, period by period, the CLAUSE ARCHITECTURE below --- the same inventory and nesting of clauses (main / relative / adverbial / complement / coordinate, to the stated depth). The WORD ORDER and the words themselves are entirely yours; only the clause skeleton is fixed.
Reproduce it for all 10 periods, in this order:
Period 1 (~8 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 2 (~29 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); 1 adverbial clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 3 (~3 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 4 (~15 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 5 (~11 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 adverbial clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; subordination nested up to depth 2.
Period 6 (~9 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 relative/adnominal clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); subordination nested up to depth 2.
Period 7 (~12 words) clause architecture: 1 adverbial clause; 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.
Period 8 (~18 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; subordination nested up to depth 0.
Period 9 (~19 words) clause architecture: 2 relative/adnominal clause; 1 main clause; 1 finite complement clause; 1 open complement (infinitive); subordination nested up to depth 4.
Period 10 (~9 words) clause architecture: 1 main clause; 1 finite complement clause; subordination nested up to depth 1.

TARGET SCENARIO --- render the content here (in your own words):
  - a hospital emergency room at a busy hour
  - the triage desk, the waiting chairs, the gurneys along the corridor
  - nurses and a doctor moving between bays; monitors, drips, a curtain drawn
  - a patient in distress and a companion; a complaint about the wait
  - the register of clinical urgency: intercom pages, wristbands, forms

REQUIREMENTS --- both hold together:
1. CLAUSE ARCHITECTURE PRESERVED --- the same clause inventory and nesting depth per period, in any word order and words you choose.
2. COHERENT --- one continuous, fully sensible passage in the target scenario; new lexicon,
   no trace of any source content.

Write modern, natural English. Produce the 10 periods in order as continuous prose --- no
numbering, no headings. Output ONLY the passage: no preamble, no self-audit.

gens.text: The doors opened onto a wall of noise. A weary nurse hurried to reach the triage desk before the intercom paged again, though the corridor already sagged under the weight of waiting bodies. Someone groaned. The man on the third gurney, whose wristband had smeared, clutched at his ribs. When the monitor beeped in the bay that the doctor had just left, a drip kept dripping. The woman who rose from her chair began to shout. Because no one answered her quickly enough, her companion slumped against the cold wall. The forms on the clipboard demanded a signature that trembling fingers could not quite manage in the crowded, humming light. A younger nurse, who moved between the drawn curtains that hid the sickest cases, whispered that the wait would stretch on to swallow the whole aching night. She promised, softly, that help was coming.

The doors slid open and the noise arrived. A nurse crossed the corridor to reach the triage desk, where wristbands lay in bright coils, before she paused above a gurney whose occupant stirred. Monitors blinked. A doctor at the far bay studied the drip that dangled from its silver hook. When a curtain slid closed around a patient who moaned, the companion rose. The woman waiting near the chairs began to protest quietly. Because the intercom paged a code overhead, the corridor emptied of loitering staff. Someone had left a clipboard of unsigned forms balanced on the arm of a plastic chair beneath the flickering wall clock. The man who clutched his chest, who had waited past the hour that the sign near the desk promised meant something, insisted that he could not breathe. Everyone understood that the night was only beginning.

The sliding doors gasped open again. A nurse hurried past the triage desk to reach the far bay, where the monitors kept their impatient counting. She clipped a wristband on. The woman in the third chair, who had waited since noon, pressed a form flat against her knee. Because the corridor filled with gurneys, the man who groaned there went unseen for a while. His companion rose, wanting to flag someone down. When the intercom paged a code overhead, two attendants broke into a run. The drawn curtain hid a doctor threading a fresh drip line into a shaking forearm under the fluorescent glare. The patient whose lips had gone gray whispered that he feared the pressure that was building in his chest would refuse to stop. The companion insisted that the wait had grown unforgivable.

The doors slid open again. She wheeled the gurney forward to reach the triage desk, though the corridor was already crowded with waiting bodies. Someone paged overhead. A nurse in blue scrubs checked the wristband that the last arrival wore. Because the monitors kept beeping, she adjusted a drip that hung above the man. He struggled to breathe behind the curtain they had drawn. When the doctor finally appeared, the companion demanded an explanation. The forms on the clipboard listed symptoms, allergies, medications, and a scrawled name barely legible under the fluorescent lights. The woman who sat clutching her husband's coat believed that the staff, who hurried between bays, had somehow forgotten to notice their hours of quiet suffering. She whispered that the pain was worsening now.

The doors slid open with a hiss. A nurse stepped forward to greet the newcomers, though the corridor already bristled with gurneys, and the triage desk hummed under its stack of forms. Wristbands waited. The doctor who crossed between the curtained bays paused only to check a failing monitor. Before she could reach the drip that dangled near the far wall, an alarm shrilled. The companion rose, needing to explain the wait. Because the waiting chairs had filled by dusk, tempers frayed against the pages. An intercom voice summoned another team to the third bay in a flat, insistent tone. The man who clutched his ticket demanded that someone tell him whether the woman who lay behind the curtain would live to see morning. The clerk answered that the forms must come first.

The double doors sighed open again. A nurse crossed the corridor to reach the triage desk, though the waiting chairs had already filled beyond their capacity. Monitors beeped. A doctor who had been paged twice finally emerged from behind the drawn curtain. When a gurney rolled past the bays where the drips hung silent, an orderly steadied it. The patient in bay four struggled to breathe. Because his companion demanded answers, a clerk explained the wait. The intercom announced a code somewhere upstairs. A woman clutched her freshly printed wristband while the forms slid from her lap and scattered across the polished floor and nobody stopped to gather them. The daughter who stood beside the man whose chart the resident scanned insisted that someone must come to help him now. Everyone knew that the night had only begun.

The doors hissed open once more. A nurse hurried past the triage desk to reach the far bay, because the monitor there had begun its shrill alarm. Wristbands piled up. The clerk who guarded the forms called out a name that no one answered. When the intercom paged a surgeon whose voice cracked over the corridor, the waiting chairs stiffened. The woman who clutched her son wanted to scream. Although the drip had emptied, a doctor lingered elsewhere. The gurneys stretched along the wall in a long patient row, each one bearing a body wrapped in thin blankets and quiet dread. The companion, who feared the worst and who begged for someone to notice, muttered that the wait had swallowed an hour. She saw that no curtain moved.

The night shift swallowed the emergency room whole.

A nurse at the triage desk paused to weigh each arrival, glancing at wristbands as the intercom paged another team toward the far bays.

Monitors chirped steadily.

The gurneys that lined the corridor held patients half-asleep beneath thin blankets.

Because the wait had stretched long, a woman whose husband slumped in his chair began to worry.

The doctor who crossed between curtains stopped to check a drip.

When a monitor's alarm suddenly rose, three nurses converged around the bed.

A drawn curtain concealed the quiet, careful work of hands adjusting tubes and pressing gauze against a wound.

The clerk who guarded the clipboards, which no one had returned, insisted that the anxious companion understand she must first complete the forms.

Somewhere down the hall a voice announced that another ambulance was arriving.

The doors slid open on chaos. A nurse hurried past the triage desk to reach the far bay, where a monitor had begun shrieking its thin electronic alarm. The corridor was full. Gurneys lined the wall, each one bearing a patient whose face had gone slack with exhaustion. When the intercom paged a doctor who was already elbow-deep in another crisis, the waiting room stirred. Somewhere behind a curtain, a drip needed changing. Because the wait had stretched past three hours, a companion approached the desk to complain. The clerk answered with the flat, apologetic patience of someone who has said the same words a thousand times before. A man clutching a wristband he had been given at eleven, whose wife lay shivering in a chair that offered no comfort, insisted that he needed to speak with someone in charge. Everyone understood that the night was only beginning.

The intercom crackled above the crowded floor. A nurse hurried past the triage desk to reach the far bay, where a monitor had begun its shrill, insistent alarm. Curtains hung still. The doctor, who was threading through the gurneys along the corridor, paused only briefly. Because the waiting room was full, a man whose wife lay pale clutched a clipboard tightly. He rose to demand attention, needing someone to listen. When the clerk glanced up, she promised nothing certain. The wristband on the woman's arm glowed under the harsh fluorescent panels that buzzed relentlessly overhead. A young intern, who checked the drip that dangled beside her chair, murmured that the swelling would ease once the medication took hold. Everyone understood that the night had only begun.
